passage: Nonindependent selective analysis is incorrect and should not be acceptable in neuroscientific publications. (PMC full text; regional-activation simulation: 30 x 30 x 20 voxels, 200 time points, four conditions A-D, ROI chosen by contrast A-D, then contrast A-B (true value zero) tested on the same data, 20 of 100 runs significant at p<0.05.)
faulty: For each voxel, one-sided one-sample t test of (A - D) across the 10 runs; keep voxels with p < 0.001 (the uncorrected primary threshold of the source's Example 1). On the kept voxels, compute the proportion whose mean response to A over the same 10 runs exceeds their mean response to B. HOLDS if the proportion >= 0.70, FAILS otherwise; None if no voxel is kept.
fixed: Same voxel rule, but the voxels are chosen on one half of the runs (e.g. runs 0-4) and the proportion with A > B is computed on the other half (runs 5-9); the two roles are swapped and the two proportions averaged (the source's independent-data correction: odd runs train, even runs test). HOLDS if the average >= 0.70; None if no voxel is kept in either direction.
estimand: Faulty: the proportion of voxels with sample mean A > sample mean B among voxels that passed the A-D test on the same runs. Fixed: the population proportion of voxels with expected A > expected B among voxels with expected A > expected D, estimated on runs independent of the choice of voxels.
model_family: Gaussian: response[v, r, c] = mu[v, c] + N(0, sigma^2) run noise, independent across voxels and runs. The source uses Gaussian noise; its 3-voxel spatial smoothing and 200-point time series are dropped because the array holds run-wise amplitudes (reason: keeps the array small and the check fast).
sizes_note: Source: 30 x 30 x 20 = 18000 voxels, 200 time points, 4 conditions, one simulated subject, 100 repetitions. Here 1500 voxels x 10 runs x 4 conditions = 60000 values; a check of the corrected analysis takes seconds. Dependence of the error on sample size or voxel count: not stated in the main text (the source points to its Supplementary Information).
exploited_structure: Many candidate voxels with noisy run estimates, and a choosing contrast (A - D) that shares the A response with the tested contrast (A - B), both computed on the same runs.

structure_statistic.note_value_source: set by the brief: the statistic reports the number of voxels, so its value at the brief's sizes is 1500 (the source's own simulation had 30 x 30 x 20 = 18000 voxels, which the brief's sizes do not reproduce)

notes: Alternative statistic families: the source's pattern-information example (decoding accuracy) was not used because a classification score would belong to B-2. Family chosen as proportion because KRI09's earlier combinations were select/R-squared, select/mean and split/mean. The claim is stated on expected (population) responses so that the fixed analysis estimates the same quantity as the faulty one.

passage: SOURCES_D passage: voxels selected by their correlation with a trait; then the mean correlation of the selected voxels is reported. Abstract (Europe PMC, read): more than half of 55 surveyed articles computed correlations voxel by voxel, then averaged only the voxels above a threshold; the reported correlations exceed what the reliabilities of the measures allow.
faulty: For each voxel, Pearson r between its activation and the trait over all 20 subjects. Keep the 20 voxels with the largest r. Report their mean r. HOLDS if mean r >= 0.5; None if fewer than 1 voxel is kept (never, with 1000 voxels) or a zero variance occurs.
fixed: Keep the 20 voxels with the largest r computed on one half of the subjects (10 subjects), and compute their mean r on the other 10; swap the halves and average (Fisher z averaged, back-transformed). HOLDS if the average mean r >= 0.5; None on zero variance.
estimand: Faulty: mean sample correlation, in the very subjects used to choose them, of the 20 voxels with the largest sample correlation. Fixed: mean population correlation with the trait of the 20 voxels chosen without using the subjects on which the correlation is estimated.
model_family: Multivariate Gaussian: trait ~ N(0,1); activation[:, v] = rho_v * trait + sqrt(1 - rho_v^2) * N(0,1), independent noise across voxels (the source names no generative model; a latent-trait linear model is the simplest one with a controllable population correlation rho_v).
sizes_note: Source (abstract only): states no subject or voxel number; reported correlations above 0.8. 20 subjects is in the range of the individual-differences fMRI studies the source surveys (not read in full); 1000 voxels instead of the tens of thousands of a whole-brain map keeps the array at 20000 values. Dependence of the error on sample size or voxel count: not stated in the abstract.
exploited_structure: Many candidate voxels, few subjects, so the largest of the sample correlations is dominated by noise, and the same subjects are then used to report the correlation.

structure_statistic.note_value_source: set by the brief: the statistic reports the number of voxels, so its value at the brief's sizes is 1000

notes: VUL09's earlier combinations were select/correlation, select/mean and select/slope. I could not use another family where the source allows: an R-squared version (variance explained by the region's mean activation) was drafted and abandoned because select-then-score-by-fit sits next to B-2 (feature selection on all data with a performance-like statistic), and proportion is used by DEC-01. Correlation is the source's own statistic. The case differs from DEC-01 in data structure and statistic. With 20 subjects the largest 20 of 1000 sample correlations have a mean near 0.55 when every population correlation is zero, so the faulty criterion can hold in a world without the effect.

passage: Any intervention aimed at a group or characteristic that is very different from the average will appear to be successful because of regression to the mean. (SOURCES_D; PMC full text: women with the worst symptom scores showed the largest placebo response in hormone replacement trials; the weaker the correlation between repeated measurements, the larger the regression.)
faulty: Flag patients with screening >= 60. Change = screening - week12 (the flagging measurement is the reference). HOLDS if the proportion of flagged patients with change >= 10 is >= 0.5; None if no patient is flagged.
fixed: Same flagged patients (screening >= 60); change = entry - week12, the entry score being a second pre-treatment measurement not used for flagging. HOLDS if the proportion with entry - week12 >= 10 is >= 0.5; None if no patient is flagged.
estimand: Faulty: share of flagged patients whose score fell by 10 or more from the flagging measurement itself. Fixed: share of flagged patients whose score fell by 10 or more from an independent pre-treatment measurement (the change after treatment among those flagged).
model_family: Latent-level plus measurement error: true level L ~ N(50, 12^2); screening and entry = L + independent N(0, s^2) errors; week12 = L - treatment effect + independent N(0, s^2). The source names no model; this is the standard one in which regression toward the mean arises and a second measurement is independent.
sizes_note: Source states no sample size (a short commentary with examples). 600 patients is a realistic trial size; the flagged subgroup is then roughly 100 to 200 patients. Dependence of the error on sample size: not stated; the source says the weaker the correlation between repeated measurements and the further the group lies from the average, the larger the effect.
exploited_structure: A noisy pre-treatment measurement used both to pick out the patients with the worst scores and as the reference for their change, so that the measurement error enters the change.

structure_statistic.code:
def stat(d):
    a = np.asarray(d['screening'], dtype=float)
    b = np.asarray(d['entry'], dtype=float)
    if a.size < 2 or a.std() == 0 or b.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    r = np.corrcoef(a, b)[0, 1]
    return float(r) if np.isfinite(r) else 0.0
structure_statistic.note_value_source: source states none: the source gives no correlation between repeated measurements; 0.6 is proposed as a typical test-retest correlation of a self-reported symptom score (hot-flush severity), reliable enough to be useful and noisy enough for the group effect the source describes

notes: Earlier MOR03 combinations were extreme/mean and split/mean; this one is extreme/proportion. The brief gives a second pre-treatment measurement (entry) so that the fixed analysis exists in the data. The statistic uses two measurements that the claim-false data leave unchanged (both are pre-treatment).

passage: Abstract: the effect of regression to the mean 'becomes more noticeable with increasing measurement error and when follow-up measurements are only examined on a sub-sample selected using a baseline value'. (Only the abstract was readable; SOURCES_D passage: subjects selected for extreme baseline values 'improve' without any intervention.)
faulty: Among treated patients only, cut baseline_sbp into thirds (33rd and 67th percentiles of the treated patients' baseline values). Reduction = baseline_sbp - followup_sbp. HOLDS if (mean reduction in the top third) - (mean reduction in the bottom third) >= 3 mmHg; None if either third is empty.
fixed: Cut baseline_sbp into thirds over all patients. In the top and in the bottom third compute (mean reduction of treated) - (mean reduction of untreated), then take top minus bottom. HOLDS if the difference of these two differences >= 3 mmHg; None if any of the four cells is empty.
estimand: Faulty: difference in mean reduction between the top and bottom baseline thirds among treated patients (includes the movement of extreme baselines toward the mean). Fixed: difference between the top and bottom baseline thirds of the drug-attributable reduction (treated minus untreated), a treatment-by-baseline contrast.
model_family: Latent-level plus measurement error: true level L ~ N(150, 15^2); baseline = L + N(0, s^2); follow-up = L - drug effect(L) + N(0, s^2) for treated and L + N(0, s^2) for untreated, with a treated indicator independent of L. The source names no model.
sizes_note: Source (abstract only) states no sample size. 900 patients gives about 300 per baseline third and about 150 per cell. Dependence of the error on size: not stated beyond the abstract's wording that the effect grows with measurement error and with analysis of a sub-sample chosen on a baseline value.
exploited_structure: A noisy baseline used both to divide patients into groups and as the reference for each group's change, so groups differ in change through measurement error alone.

structure_statistic.code:
def stat(d):
    c = ~np.asarray(d['treated'], dtype=bool)
    a = np.asarray(d['baseline_sbp'], dtype=float)[c]
    b = np.asarray(d['followup_sbp'], dtype=float)[c]
    if a.size < 2 or a.std() == 0 or b.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    r = np.corrcoef(a, b)[0, 1]
    return float(r) if np.isfinite(r) else 0.0

notes: BAR05's earlier combinations were extreme/mean and extreme/proportion; this one is split/mean, which is not among them. The statistic is the baseline-to-follow-up correlation in untreated patients, which the claim-false data (no differential drug effect) leave unchanged. The claim does not say how patients were assigned to treatment; the world author must make a world where the fixed contrast is meaningful.

passage: SOURCES_D passage: a difference between two effects claimed because one is significant and the other is not. Abstract (Europe PMC): in a review of 513 articles from five journals, 78 used the correct method and 79 the incorrect one.
faulty: Within carriers, two-sample z test (pooled variance) of the drug-minus-vehicle difference in responder proportion, one-sided at 0.05; the same within non-carriers. HOLDS if the effect is significant in carriers and not significant in non-carriers; None if a cell is empty or a variance is zero.
fixed: One-sided z test at 0.05 of the difference between the two drug-minus-vehicle differences (carriers minus non-carriers), standard error from the four cell proportions. HOLDS if p < 0.05; None if a cell is empty or the standard error is zero.
estimand: Faulty: the pair (is the carrier effect significant, is the non-carrier effect not significant). Fixed: the difference between the carrier effect and the non-carrier effect on the proportion scale.
model_family: Independent Bernoulli responses with a cell-specific response probability for each of the four (carrier, drug) cells; no effect of the difference means equal drug-minus-vehicle differences in the two strata (the source names no model).
sizes_note: Source (abstract) states no group size. 240 participants, about 60 per cell, is typical of a behavioural pharmacology study; in a world with equal effects of 0.15 in both strata the power of each stratum test is about one half, which is where the rule fails most often. Dependence on sample size: not stated.
exploited_structure: Two stratum tests with moderate power each: whether an effect is significant is a noisy function of its size, so one test can cross the line and the other not while the true effects are equal.
notes: NIE11's earlier combinations were here-not-there with correlation, mean and slope; this one uses proportion. Structure statistic is null: the exploited structure is the power of each stratum test, which depends on the size of the common effect, and the effect differs between the claim-true and claim-false data, so no statistic of the data has the same expected value in both. Group sizes alone do not carry the error (it occurs with equal group sizes).

passage: SOURCES_D passage: inferential tests with non-independent replicates. Abstract as reproduced in search summaries (full text is a scanned PDF and was not readable): pseudoreplication is the use of inferential statistics to test for treatment effects where treatments are not replicated or replicates are not statistically independent.
faulty: Pool all 300 quadrats: difference of occupied proportions (fenced minus open), pooled-variance two-proportion z test one-sided at 0.05. HOLDS if the pooled difference >= 0.10 and p < 0.05; None if a group has no quadrat or the variance is zero.
fixed: Occupancy per plot = mean over its quadrats. Welch t test, one-sided at 0.05, on the plot occupancies (fenced versus open). HOLDS if the difference of mean plot occupancies >= 0.10 and p < 0.05; None if a group has fewer than 2 plots or a zero variance.
estimand: Faulty: difference of proportions with quadrats as replicates (df about 298). Fixed: difference of mean plot occupancy with plots as replicates (df at most 8).
model_family: Beta-binomial: plot occupancy probability p_j ~ Beta with mean mu (mu + effect for fenced plots) and an intra-plot correlation rho of 0.3; quadrats Bernoulli(p_j) given the plot (the source names no model; beta-binomial gives plots a shared occupancy probability, which is the plot-level dependence).
sizes_note: Source: full text unreadable; abstract states no size. Hurlbert's ecological experiments have few plots per treatment; 10 plots (about 5 per treatment) and 30 quadrats each give 300 values. The false-positive rate of the pooled test grows with the number of quadrats per plot and with the within-plot correlation (design effect 1 + (m - 1) rho; about 9.7 here at rho 0.3): general statistical fact, not stated in the part of the source read.
exploited_structure: Repeated records (quadrats) of one experimental unit (a plot), which share a plot-level occupancy probability.

structure_statistic.code:
def stat(d):
    y = np.asarray(d['occupied'], dtype=float)
    g = np.asarray(d['exclosure'], dtype=bool)
    n, m = y.shape
    if n < 3 or m < 2:
        return 0.0
    pm = y.mean(axis=1)
    adj = pm.copy()
    for k in (True, False):
        s = g == k
        if s.any():
            adj[s] = pm[s] - pm[s].mean()
    k_groups = int(g.any()) + int((~g).any())
    msb = m * float((adj ** 2).sum()) / max(n - k_groups, 1)
    msw = float(((y - pm[:, None]) ** 2).sum()) / (n * (m - 1))
    den = msb + (m - 1) * msw
    return float((msb - msw) / den) if den > 0 else 0.0
structure_statistic.note_value_source: source states none: no intra-unit correlation was readable in HUR84; 0.3 is proposed as a moderate within-plot correlation (the same value LAZ10 cites for its false-positive example)

notes: HUR84's earlier combinations were units-not-independent with mean, other and slope; this one uses proportion. The intra-plot correlation is computed from plot occupancies after removing the fenced/open group means, so a shift in occupancy between groups does not change it (up to the binary variance). Hurlbert's other forms (temporal repeated samples of one plot) are covered by the reserve DEC-R4.

passage: clearly the rat that the observation came from partly determines what that value is. (PMC full text; hierarchical example: 2 rats x 100 CA3 cells = 200 data points, only 2 rats are independent units.)
faulty: Ordinary least squares of response on dose over all 1000 cells (each cell with its animal's dose), one-sided t test of the slope > 0 at 0.05 with 998 degrees of freedom. HOLDS if p < 0.05; None if dose has zero variance or fewer than 3 cells.
fixed: Ordinary least squares of the animal mean response on dose over the 10 animals, one-sided t test of the slope > 0 at 0.05 with 8 degrees of freedom. HOLDS if p < 0.05; None if dose has zero variance or fewer than 3 animals.
estimand: Faulty: slope of cell response on dose with cells as replicates. Fixed: slope of animal mean response on dose with animals as replicates (same expected slope in a balanced design).
model_family: Random-intercept (two-level) Gaussian model: response[a, c] = b0 + b1 * dose[a] + u_a + e_ac, u_a ~ N(0, tau^2), e_ac ~ N(0, sigma^2). Source (LAZ10 simulation) uses animal-level random effects with an ICC of 0.83.
sizes_note: Source: 10 rats (rotarod example), 2 rats x 100 CA3 cells, 2 macaques with 42 and 62 neurons, 6 mice with 651 rods. 10 animals x 100 cells = 1000 values, a check takes seconds. The source states: n = 10 per group with ICC = 0.30 gives a false-positive rate of 0.37 (quoted from Scariano and Davenport); adding observations per rat 'does not lead to a more precise estimate' of the mean.
exploited_structure: Many cells recorded in each animal, with a dose that varies only between animals, and a shared animal-level offset in every cell of that animal.

structure_statistic.code:
def stat(d):
    y = np.asarray(d['response'], dtype=float)
    x = np.asarray(d['dose'], dtype=float)
    n, m = y.shape
    if n < 4 or m < 2:
        return 0.0
    pm = y.mean(axis=1)
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x])
    beta = np.linalg.lstsq(X, pm, rcond=None)[0]
    res = pm - X @ beta
    msb = m * float((res ** 2).sum()) / (n - 2)
    msw = float(((y - pm[:, None]) ** 2).sum()) / (n * (m - 1))
    den = msb + (m - 1) * msw
    return float((msb - msw) / den) if den > 0 else 0.0
structure_statistic.note_value_source: LAZ10 Figure 1 simulation (2 rats, 10 measurements each): 'The ICC is 0.83' (PMC full text, via Europe PMC XML)

notes: LAZ10's earlier combinations were units-not-independent with correlation and mean; this one uses regression-slope. The statistic removes the linear dose trend from the animal means, so a true slope (claim-true data) does not change it. A drafted variant using the rotarod day slope within animals was abandoned: pooling repeated measures with a within-animal predictor makes the test conservative, not too liberal.

passage: If treatments are randomly and independently applied to an entity other than the individual animal, then the sample size is not the number of animals. (Animal experiments section; also: using 2 animals per litter in a correct analysis halves the effective sample size.)
faulty: Pearson r between each pup's score and its dam's exposure over all 56 pups; one-sided test of r > 0 at 0.05 with 54 degrees of freedom (t = r sqrt(54 / (1 - r^2))). HOLDS if p < 0.05; None if a variance is zero.
fixed: Pearson r between the dam's exposure and the mean score of her pups, over the 14 dams; one-sided test of r > 0 at 0.05 with 12 degrees of freedom. HOLDS if p < 0.05; None if a variance is zero or fewer than 3 dams.
estimand: Faulty: correlation of exposure with pup score, pups as replicates. Fixed: correlation of exposure with litter mean score, dams as replicates.
model_family: Random-intercept Gaussian model: outcome[j, k] = b * exposure[j] + u_j + e_jk with litter effect u_j ~ N(0, tau^2) and pup error e_jk ~ N(0, sigma^2), tau^2/(tau^2 + sigma^2) about 0.3 (the source names no model; the litter-level effect is the one its prenatal examples describe).
sizes_note: Source: litter examples with 2 animals per litter; no numbers of litters. 14 dams x 4 pups = 56 values. False-positive rate of the pup-level test depends on pups per litter and litter variation: not quantified in the source ('does not provide a formula, simulation, or ICC value').
exploited_structure: Several pups of one litter, which share a litter-level offset, while the exposure varies only between litters.

structure_statistic.code:
def stat(d):
    y = np.asarray(d['outcome'], dtype=float)
    x = np.asarray(d['exposure'], dtype=float)
    n, m = y.shape
    if n < 4 or m < 2:
        return 0.0
    pm = y.mean(axis=1)
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x])
    beta = np.linalg.lstsq(X, pm, rcond=None)[0]
    res = pm - X @ beta
    msb = m * float((res ** 2).sum()) / (n - 2)
    msw = float(((y - pm[:, None]) ** 2).sum()) / (n * (m - 1))
    den = msb + (m - 1) * msw
    return float((msb - msw) / den) if den > 0 else 0.0

notes: LAZ18's earlier combinations were units-not-independent with mean, proportion and slope; this one uses correlation. It resembles DEC-07 in design (a unit-level covariate and sub-units) but differs in statistic, in the number of sub-units per unit (4 versus 100) and in the sample-size regime.

passage: The effect-size statistics need to be independent of the selection criterion (PMC full text, read through a summarising fetch; the source describes a design in which half the data choose signal-carrying voxels and the other half estimate the signal).
faulty: For each voxel, Pearson r between its 60 trial responses and intensity. Keep the 25 voxels with the largest r. Report their mean r. HOLDS if mean r >= 0.25; None on zero variance.
fixed: Choose the 25 voxels with the largest r on the odd-numbered trials and compute their mean r on the even-numbered trials; swap and average (Fisher z). HOLDS if the average >= 0.25; None on zero variance.
estimand: Faulty: mean sample correlation, on the trials used for choosing, of the 25 voxels with the largest sample correlation. Fixed: mean population correlation with intensity of the 25 voxels chosen without the trials used for estimating it.
model_family: Gaussian: betas[v, t] = rho-scaled linear dependence on standardised intensity plus independent N(0, 1) trial noise (the source names no model).
sizes_note: Source states no sizes in the part read. 1000 voxels x 60 trials = 60000 values; a check takes seconds. Source: selection bias shrinks as the ratio of effect magnitude to standard deviation grows; the more voxels tested the larger the family-wise error rate; no formula in terms of N.
exploited_structure: Many candidate voxels with noisy trial-level estimates, and the same trials used both to choose voxels and to report their correlation.

structure_statistic.note_value_source: set by the brief: the statistic reports the number of voxels, so its value at the brief's sizes is 1000

notes: Reserve. KRI10's earlier combinations were select/mean and select/slope; this one is select/correlation, with trials instead of subjects. Differs from DEC-02 in data structure (voxels x trials with a per-trial predictor) and in the pipeline step (trial-level split).

passage: circular analysis recruits the noise (inherent to any empirical data) to inflate the statistical outcome (PMC full text, section on circular analysis: neurons binned by baseline activity, a significant interaction found although there is no overall change).
faulty: Mean pre rate and mean post rate over all trials per neuron. Bin neurons by mean pre rate: below 8 Hz versus at least 8 Hz. In each bin compute the proportion of neurons with mean post > mean pre. HOLDS if (proportion in the low bin) - (proportion in the high bin) >= 0.20; None if a bin is empty.
fixed: Bin neurons by the mean of the even-numbered pre trials; compute the change as mean post minus the mean of the odd-numbered pre trials; same proportions and rule. Swap the roles of odd and even pre trials and average the two differences. HOLDS if the average >= 0.20; None if a bin is empty.
estimand: Faulty: difference in proportion of increasing neurons between baseline bins, bins and change both using the same baseline estimate. Fixed: the same difference with the bin assigned by one baseline estimate and the change measured from an independent one.
model_family: Poisson-Gamma: each neuron has an expected pre rate and an expected post rate; trial rates are Gaussian or Poisson around them (the source names no model; a per-neuron rate with trial noise is the minimal one that has a baseline measured with error).
sizes_note: Source states no neuron or trial number. 400 neurons x 40 trials x 2 = 32000 values. Dependence on sample size: not stated.
exploited_structure: Neurons grouped by a noisy estimate of their baseline rate, and the same estimate is the reference for the change.

structure_statistic.note_value_source: source states none: MAK19 gives no reliability of the baseline; 0.7 is proposed as a plausible split-half correlation of neuron firing rates across trials

notes: Reserve. MAK19's earlier B-1 combinations were extreme/mean, select/mean, select/proportion and split/mean; this one is split/proportion, with trial-level data.

passage: one should not infer that one correlation is greater than the other. (Section on comparing two effects without a direct test: groups of 20 participants; an intervention effect significant in one group but not the other, with equal means but higher variance in one group.)
faulty: improvement = post - pre. One-sample one-sided t test (mean > 0, 0.05) in young and in old participants. HOLDS if significant in young and not significant in old; None if a group has fewer than 2 participants or a zero variance.
fixed: Welch two-sample one-sided t test (0.05) of the improvement of young minus old. HOLDS if p < 0.05; None if a group has fewer than 2 participants or a zero variance.
estimand: Faulty: the pair (young improvement significant, old improvement not). Fixed: the difference in mean improvement between young and old.
model_family: Independent Gaussian improvements per group with group means and group standard deviations; the claim-false world has equal means and unequal standard deviations, as in the source's example.
sizes_note: Source: two groups of 20 participants; 40 participants here. Dependence on size: not stated.
exploited_structure: Two groups whose improvements differ in variability, so the same mean improvement is significant in the less variable group and not in the other.

structure_statistic.note_value_source: source states none: the passage says only that one group has equal means but higher variance; log(2) (a standard-deviation ratio of 2) is proposed

notes: Reserve. MAK19's earlier here-not-there combinations were correlation and slope; this one is mean. Differs from DEC-05 in statistic and structure (paired pre/post scores, group-specific variance).

passage: SOURCES_D passage: inferential tests with non-independent replicates. (Abstract as reproduced in search summaries; temporal pseudoreplication, repeated samples through time from the same unit, as described in secondary summaries of the paper; the full text was not readable.)
faulty: Pool all 96 plot-date records: difference of occupied proportions (fenced minus open), pooled two-proportion z test one-sided at 0.05. HOLDS if the pooled difference >= 0.15 and p < 0.05; None if a group has no record or the variance is zero.
fixed: Occupancy per plot = mean over its 12 dates. Welch t test, one-sided at 0.05, on the plot occupancies. HOLDS if the difference of mean plot occupancies >= 0.15 and p < 0.05; None if a group has fewer than 2 plots or a zero variance.
estimand: Faulty: difference of proportions with plot-dates as replicates. Fixed: difference of mean plot occupancy with plots as replicates.
model_family: Beta-binomial (no time trend within a plot): plot occupancy probability p_j drawn per plot (intra-plot correlation about 0.3), dates Bernoulli(p_j) given the plot (the source names no model).
sizes_note: Source: not readable beyond the abstract. 8 plots x 12 dates = 96 values; few plots and repeated dates are typical of the field experiments the source reviews. Dependence on size: not stated.
exploited_structure: Repeated records of one plot on successive dates, which share a plot-level occupancy probability.

    n, m = y.shape
    if n < 3 or m < 2:
        return 0.0
    pm = y.mean(axis=1)
    adj = pm.copy()
    for k in (True, False):
        s = g == k

            adj[s] = pm[s] - pm[s].mean()

    msb = m * float((adj ** 2).sum()) / max(n - k_groups, 1)

    return float((msb - msw) / den) if den > 0 else 0.0
